entities.name: Roseline de Villeneuve
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Roseline de Villeneuve (1263–1329), a French Carthusian nun and mystic, represents a significant figure in the late medieval spiritual landscape of Provence, embodying the era's fervent devotion and the evolving role of women within monasticism. Born into the noble Villeneuve family of Provence, her life, marked by profound asceticism and reported mystical experiences, solidified the Carthusian order's reputation for sanctity and provided a powerful model for female religious life in the 13th and early 14th centuries, a period characterized by intense spiritual renewal across Western Europe.

At the age of 25, Roseline defied societal expectations for noblewomen by entering the strict Carthusian monastery of Bertaud in the diocese of Gap in 1288, later becoming prioress of the Chartreuse de Celle-Roubaud near Les Arcs-sur-Argens in 1300. Her tenure as prioress was distinguished by rigorous adherence to Carthusian discipline, visions, and a legendary devotion to the poor, often depicted through miraculous multiplication of food. Her brother, Hélion de Villeneuve, Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller, was a notable contemporary who supported her monastic endeavors, underscoring the interconnectedness of noble families and religious institutions during this era.

Following her death on January 17, 1329, Roseline's tomb at Celle-Roubaud became a site of pilgrimage, with numerous miracles attributed to her intercession. Her cult spread throughout Provence and within the Carthusian order, leading to her beatification by the Catholic Church, though a formal canonization process was protracted. Her incorrupt body, discovered five years after her death, further fueled her veneration, cementing her status as a local saint and a spiritual beacon for the devout. The veneration of Roseline contributed to the broader recognition of female spiritual authority and sanctity in a male-dominated ecclesiastical structure.
